title: Longest Well-Performing Interval
statement:
`hours[i]` records how many hours an employee worked on day `i`. Call a day *tiring* when its value is more than 8 (a value of exactly 8 is not tiring).

A run of consecutive days is *well-performing* if it contains strictly more tiring days than non-tiring days. Return the length of the longest well-performing run, or `0` if there is none.
notes:
## Intuition

Replace each day by `+1` if it is tiring and `-1` otherwise. A run is well-performing exactly when its values sum to something positive. Checking every run is O(n²). With a running prefix total `score`, the run after index `i` up to `day` has sum `score(day) - score(i)`, so we want the earliest earlier prefix that is smaller than the current one.

Because `score` moves by exactly 1 each day and starts at 0, two cases cover everything. If `score > 0`, the whole prefix `0..day` already works. Otherwise any smaller prefix value must have passed through `score - 1` first, so the earliest index where `score - 1` appeared gives the longest run ending at `day`.

## Approach

1. Keep `score` (tiring minus non-tiring days so far) and a map `firstSeen` from each score value to the first day it occurred.
2. For each `day`, add `+1` or `-1` to `score`.
3. If `score > 0`, the run from day 0 is well-performing: `best = day + 1`.
4. Otherwise, if `score - 1` was seen at day `j`, the run `j+1..day` has sum 1; update `best` with `day - j`.
5. Record `day` for `score` only if this value is new, keeping the earliest index.

## Example 1, step by step

`hours = [9, 9, 6, 0, 6, 6, 9]`. Scores after each day: `1, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -1`.
Days 0–2 have positive scores, so `best` becomes 1, 2, then 3. At day 3 (`score = 0`), `-1` is not seen yet. At day 4 (`-1`), `-2` is unseen; `-1` is stored at day 4. At day 5 (`-2`), `-3` is unseen; `-2` is stored at day 5. At day 6 (`-1`), `-2` was first seen at day 5, a run of length 1. The answer stays `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant-time map operations.
- Space: O(n) for `firstSeen` (at most n + 1 distinct scores).

## Pitfalls

- A day with exactly 8 hours is not tiring; the test is `> 8`.
- Store only the first index of each score; overwriting it shortens the runs you find.
- Look up `score - 1`, not any smaller value: it is always the earliest smaller prefix.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `firstSeen` | score value → first day it occurred |
| `score` | tiring days minus non-tiring days in `0..day` |
| `best` | longest well-performing run found so far |
| `day` | the current day index |
